lesson.title: Tuning In: How Band-Pass Filters Isolate a Range
lesson.summary: A band-pass filter passes a range of frequencies centered on a resonant frequency while attenuating everything above and below it, combining the resonance behavior of an RLC circuit with the bandwidth language used across all filters.
lesson.body:
A band-pass filter's passband is not below or above a single cutoff, it is a band sandwiched between a lower cutoff frequency fL and an upper cutoff frequency fH, with stopbands on both sides. The width of that passband, fH minus fL, is the bandwidth introduced in Bandwidth, and the center of the band is usually set by resonance, the phenomenon from Resonance.

The classic way to build a band-pass filter is a series RLC circuit with the output taken across the resistor. In a series RLC circuit, the inductor's reactance ωL and the capacitor's reactance 1/(ωC) point in opposite directions and cancel exactly at the resonant frequency ω0 = 1/√(LC). At resonance the circuit's total impedance is just R, so essentially all of the source voltage appears across R and the output is close to Vin, near-total passage. Move away from resonance in either direction and the net reactance, whichever of ωL or 1/(ωC) now dominates, grows, the total impedance climbs above R, and less of the source voltage is left over to appear across the output resistor, so the output falls off on both sides. That is exactly the band-pass shape.

The width of the passband is set by how much resistance is in the loop relative to the inductance: bandwidth in Hz equals R/(2πL). The selectivity of the filter, how narrow and sharp the passband is relative to its center frequency, is measured by the quality factor Q = f0/BW = (1/R)√(L/C). A high-Q band-pass filter, like the one used to tune in a single radio station, has a narrow passband, a low-Q one is broad.

Take R = 50 Ω, L = 10 mH, C = 100 nF. The center frequency is f0 = 1/(2π√(LC)). LC = 0.01 times 100 times 10 to the minus 9, which is 1 times 10 to the minus 9, its square root is 3.162 times 10 to the minus 5, so f0 = 1/(2π times 3.162 times 10 to the minus 5), about 5033 Hz, roughly 5.03 kHz. The bandwidth is BW = R/(2πL) = 50/(2π times 0.01) = 50/0.06283, about 796 Hz. The quality factor is Q = f0/BW = 5033/796, about 6.3, which you can also confirm from Q = (1/R)√(L/C) = (1/50)√(0.01/1 times 10 to the minus 7) = (1/50)(316.2), about 6.3. Both routes agree, so this filter passes a roughly 796 Hz wide band centered near 5.03 kHz.
